front_blocks.md: Define **litmus**.

back_blocks.md: **Litmus** is a two-colour indicator extracted from lichens that turns **red** in acid and **blue** in alkali.

cards.front_md: Define **litmus**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Litmus is a suitable indicator for acid-alkali titrations.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Litmus is not suitable for titrations because its colour change is not sharp and it passes through a **purple** transition colour near neutral, making the **endpoint** difficult to identify.

front_blocks.md: Why are **synthetic indicators** used in acid-alkali titrations instead of litmus?

back_blocks.md: Synthetic indicators are used because they produce a **sharp colour change** at the endpoint, making it easy to identify exactly when neutralisation has occurred. Litmus changes colour gradually and passes through a purple stage, so the endpoint is hard to pinpoint.

front_blocks.md: What is the **pH scale**?

back_blocks.md: The **pH scale** is a numerical scale from 0 to 14 used to show how **acidic** or **alkaline** a solution is. It measures the amount of **hydrogen ions** present in solution.

back_blocks.md: Acids have pH values **below** 7, alkalis have pH values **above** 7, and a neutral solution has a pH of **7**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A solution with a pH of 2 is a strong acid.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
A pH of 0–3 indicates a **strong acid**. The lower the pH, the more **acidic** the solution. Extremely acidic substances can have pH values below 1.

front_blocks.md: What is **universal indicator**?

back_blocks.md: **Universal indicator** is a wide-range indicator made from a mixture of different plant **indicators**. It gives an approximate pH value by changing colour across a broad pH range, and the colour is matched to a **colour chart** to estimate the pH of an unknown solution.

front_blocks.md: Why is **universal indicator** not suitable for acid-alkali titrations?

back_blocks.md: Universal indicator is not suitable for titrations because it cannot produce a **sharp colour change** at the endpoint. A titration requires an exact endpoint, so an indicator that changes colour gradually cannot reliably show when neutralisation is complete.

front_blocks.md: What is an **acid**?

back_blocks.md: An **acid** is a substance that, when added to water, releases positively charged **hydrogen ions** (H<sup>+</sup>). The presence of H<sup>+</sup> ions is what makes a solution acidic.

front_blocks.md: What is an **alkali**?

back_blocks.md: An **alkali** is a substance that, when added to water, releases negatively charged **hydroxide ions** (OH<sup>–</sup>). The presence of OH<sup>–</sup> ions makes the solution alkaline.

front_blocks.md: What does the **pH scale** measure?

back_blocks.md: The **pH scale** measures how acidic or alkaline a solution is. It is a numerical scale that reflects the concentration of **hydrogen ions** (H<sup>+</sup>) in the solution.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
All reactions of acids count as neutralisation reactions.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

Neutralisation specifically requires an acid to react with an **alkali**, producing water. When a metal reacts with an acid, a salt is formed but no water is produced, so it is not a **neutralisation** reaction.

front_blocks.md: Define **neutralisation**.

back_blocks.md: **Neutralisation** is the reaction between an acid and an alkali in which H<sup>+</sup> ions and OH<sup>–</sup> ions combine to produce **water** (H<sub>2</sub>O). The reaction results in a neutral solution.

front_blocks.md: How is **neutralisation** used in soil treatment?

back_blocks.md: Neutralisation is used to raise the pH of acidic soils that are too acidic for some crops. Bases such as **limestone** or **quicklime** are added to the soil to neutralise the acid and increase the pH.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The equation H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + OH<sup>–</sup> (aq) → H<sub>2</sub>O (l) represents all acid-base neutralisations.

back_blocks.md: **True.**

This **net ionic equation** applies to every acid-base neutralisation. The H<sup>+</sup> and OH<sup>–</sup> ions always combine to produce **water**, regardless of which specific acid and alkali are used.

front_blocks.md: What is a **titration**?

back_blocks.md: A **titration** is a technique used to determine the **concentration** of a solution. In an acid-base titration, it measures exactly how much of one solution is needed to neutralise another.

front_blocks.md: Why is the conical flask placed on a **white tile** during a titration?

back_blocks.md: The conical flask is placed on a white tile to make it easier to see the **colour change** of the indicator at the endpoint. The white background provides contrast against the solution.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Two titration results are concordant if they are within 0.1 cm<sup>3</sup> of each other.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Two concordant results are within 0.1 cm<sup>3</sup> of each other. At least two concordant results are needed before calculating the **mean titre**.

front_blocks.md: Why is a **rough titration** performed before the accurate titrations?

back_blocks.md: The rough titration gives an approximate **endpoint** volume. This allows the accurate titrations to be performed by adding the solution drop by drop as the endpoint is approached, making the result more **precise**.

cards.front_md: Why is a **rough titration** performed before the accurate titrations?

front_blocks.md: What are **concordant results**?

back_blocks.md: **Concordant results** are two or more titration readings that are within 0.1 cm<sup>3</sup> of each other. They are used to confirm the **reliability** of the titration and are averaged to give a **mean titre**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A funnel used to fill the burette can be left in place during the titration.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
The funnel must be removed before starting the titration. If left in place, it can **drip** liquid into the burette, making the initial reading inaccurate and giving a **false** result.
